summary: Cape Enrage light on Barn Marsh Island, Bay of Fundy: built 1838, lit 1840, square wooden tower 1904; automated 1988; site closed for the 2026 season.

structures.note: First tower, 39 ft tall, the first square lighthouse in New Brunswick (LighthouseFriends). Kept on as the keeper's house after 1870 (LighthouseFriends). Its later fate is not stated in the sources read.
Second tower, completed 1869, first shown 16 November 1870; replaced by the 1904 tower (LighthouseFriends; Department report printed 1905).
Square tower with sloping sides and octagonal iron lantern painted red, 29 ft (about 9 m) to the ventilator (Department report printed 1905; CCG list gives 9.2 m).

staffing.note: Automated and de-staffed in 1988 (LighthouseFriends; Connecting Albert County).

access.note: For the 2026 season the site was to stay closed (centre board, 2026). The Lighthouse Directory says the site is open and the tower closed for the 2026 season. The sources differ.

facts.agency: Disputed. Canadian Coast Guard (Lighthouse Directory; the Coast Guard list marks the light a 'Private aid'). Province of New Brunswick (board of the Cape Enrage Interpretive Centre, 2026).

events.note: First tower built; the legislature had appropriated money after the 1837 petition (LighthouseFriends).
Light active in spring 1840, after the Partridge Island lantern and an English lantern were delayed.
Old tower declared worn out in 1868; second tower completed in 1869.
Second tower's light first shown on 16 November 1870, with a fourth-order lens.
Fog alarm building completed with an old boiler and engine from Partridge Island; whistle began 20 October 1874.
Lightning struck the south side of the tower below the lantern floor.
New fog alarm building, $1,900, housing a Champion foghorn.
Tower rebuilt as a square wooden tower with octagonal iron lantern, light 125 ft above high water, fourth-order dioptric (Department report printed 1905).
Condemned boiler replaced by one used at Halifax, reported for the nine months ended 31 March 1907.
Province of New Brunswick announced it would buy the station from the Canadian Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends). The 2026 board post calls the facility provincially owned.
Site to stay closed for the 2026 season (centre board, reported in Brunswick News). The Lighthouse Directory says the tower is closed for the 2026 season.

corrections.why: The first light was lit in spring 1840, after the lantern delay (LighthouseFriends). 1838 is the year the tower was built and the station established.
The 1870 tower kept its light until it was rebuilt in 1904 (LighthouseFriends; Department report printed 1905). No deactivation in 1870 is recorded.
LighthouseFriends and Connecting Albert County both date automation and de-staffing to 1988. The 1980 date is not supported by either.

corrections.proposed: disputed: Canadian Coast Guard (Lighthouse Directory); 'Private aid' (Coast Guard list); provincially owned (centre board, 2026)
corrections.why: The sources disagree on ownership, and the 2026 board post is the most recent statement.

corrections.proposed: closed for the 2026 season, per the centre board; the Lighthouse Directory says site open, tower closed
corrections.why: The site was to stay closed for the 2026 season. The sources differ on the grounds.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Lighthouse Directory gives 1838 as the station's establishment and the Wikidata record gives 1840 as the first light. LighthouseFriends explains that the tower was built in 1838 and not lit until spring 1840. Both dates are used: built 1838, first lit 1840.
Wikidata gives 1868 built and 1870 first lit; LighthouseFriends gives worn out in 1868, completed 1869 and lit 16 November 1870. The LighthouseFriends dates are used.
One Wikidata entry says inactive. The Coast Guard list and the Lighthouse Directory both give the light as active, and the 2026 board post does not say otherwise. The light is recorded as active.

Wikidata's 'F W' is the fixed white light shown by the 1904 tower (Department report printed 1905). The Coast Guard list and the Lighthouse Directory give a green flash every six seconds. The date of the change is not in the sources read.

The sources range from 38 to 49 m. The 1905 Department report gives 125 ft (about 38 m) above high water for the 1904 light; the Coast Guard list gives 40.7 m for the present light. The 1904 figure is used for the history and the Coast Guard figure for today.
LighthouseFriends's text has Munson paid for part of 1839 and Grieves in charge from 1844; its keeper roster gives Munson 1842 to 1844. The story follows the text and says the roster does not fit it.

notes_for_editor: (1) Ownership and status are disputed: the Coast Guard list marks the light 'Private aid'; the Lighthouse Directory names the Canadian Coast Guard as owner; the Cape Enrage Interpretive Centre board calls the facility provincially owned (2026). LighthouseFriends reports the 1994 Province purchase announcement without saying whether it was completed. A human should check the current title. (2) For 2026 the Lighthouse Directory says the site is open and the tower closed; the board says the site will not open to visitors that season. Not resolved; the story says the accounts differ. (3) The Cape Enrage website (capeenrage.ca) returned HTTP 403 to the reader and was not read. A search snippet from it says 'permanently closed'; that was not confirmed and is not used. CBC's report on the closure timed out and was not read. An editor should check both. (4) Pre-1900 Canadian sources (the Journal of the House of Assembly, the Department of Marine's 1872 and 1877 reports) are not in the corpus. Facts from them come through LighthouseFriends, which quotes them; the originals were not read. (5) Munson's dates: LighthouseFriends' text (paid for part of 1839, Grieves in 1844) and its roster (1842 to 1844) disagree; the story follows the text and says so. (6) Barbour was checked on the page image (1905 list, printed p. 158, scan 171): 'Barbour, Jas. G', Cape Enrage Light and Fog Alarm, appointed May 11, 1888, salary 800. (7) Starratt: LighthouseFriends' text has William J. Starratt (1874 and 1877 passages); its roster and 1888 account have William S. Starratt. The story uses the roster spelling. (8) The 1905 cost: the OCR reads '8916.88'; the page image shows $916.88, and the story uses that. The 1905 report gives the light's visibility as 15 miles without saying nautical miles; the story keeps the report's unit. (9) Connecting Albert County is by Annick R. Butland, managing director of Fundy's Cape Enrage (the operator). The story footnotes that and uses it only for dates, the keepers' house, and the road. (10) Chronicling America search for 'Cape Enrage' with 'lighthouse', 1838 to 1912, returned nothing usable. (11) No wrecks, rescues or deaths at sea are sourced for this station in the sources read. (12) Dennison Tate and the keepers after 1960 are named in their public roles only. The Connecting Albert County article's personal details about Tate are not used. (13) The 'Cape Enrage Adventure Centre' name differs between sources (Cape Enragé Adventure Centre, Cape Enrage Interpretive Centre, Fundy's Cape Enrage); the story uses the board's name. (14) The record's Commons photograph has no licence in the record; none added.
